name: Insulin analogs (multiple)
route: Injection under the skin by pen, syringe or pump; regular insulin can also be given IV
status: FDA-approved for type 1 and type 2 diabetes; first weekly basal insulins (icodec, efsitora) approved in 2026 for adults with type 2 diabetes
mechanism: Lab-made insulins with small structural changes that make them act faster or last longer, replacing the insulin the pancreas no longer makes in sufficient amounts
uses: Hospital treatment of high blood sugar

article.summary: Insulin analogs are modified insulins, from rapid-acting mealtime types to daily and new once-weekly basal insulins, used to treat type 1 and type 2 diabetes in the US.
article.takeaway: Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into cells, and people with type 1 diabetes cannot survive without replacing it. Analogs are versions of human insulin with small changes that make them start faster, for meals, or last longer, for steady background coverage. Keeping blood sugar near target with insulin sharply cuts eye, kidney and nerve damage, as the landmark DCCT trial showed.[^1] The main risk is **low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)**, and newer long-acting analogs lower that risk somewhat compared with older human insulins.[^2][^3] In 2026 the FDA approved the first **once-weekly** insulins, but only for adults with type 2 diabetes.[^4][^5]
glance: Many approved products, including biosimilars; weekly icodec and efsitora approved in 2026
Type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes when other drugs are not enough, pregnancy, hospital care
Injection under the skin by pen, syringe or pump; regular insulin by IV in hospitals
Insulin receptor agonists: rapid, short, intermediate, long-acting and weekly
A century of use; landmark DCCT trial; large trials comparing analogs
[Pramlintide](/peptides/pramlintide), used with mealtime insulin; [glucagon](/peptides/glucagon) for severe lows

blocks.text: Insulin is a small protein made by beta cells in the pancreas. It signals muscle, fat and liver cells to take up glucose and tells the liver to stop releasing stored sugar. Type 1 diabetes destroys the beta cells; in type 2 diabetes the body resists insulin and production gradually falls.

Human insulin injected under the skin clumps into groups of six molecules that absorb slowly and unevenly. Analogs tweak one or a few amino acids, or add a fatty-acid chain, to change that behavior: rapid-acting analogs break apart quickly to cover meals, while basal analogs release slowly or bind to albumin in the blood to provide steady background insulin.

rows: Lispro (Humalog, Admelog, Lyumjev), aspart (NovoLog, Fiasp, biosimilars), glulisine (Apidra)
Taken at meals; start within minutes and fade in a few hours; used in pumps
Slower mealtime insulin; given IV in hospitals
Background insulin lasting about half a day, often given twice daily
Once-daily background insulin lasting a day or longer
Weekly background insulin for adults with type 2 diabetes

blocks.text: Insulin detemir (Levemir) was discontinued in the US at the end of 2024. Premixed products combine an intermediate and a rapid component in one injection.

In the DCCT, people with type 1 diabetes on intensive insulin therapy had a 76% lower risk of developing eye disease than those on conventional treatment, along with less kidney and nerve damage, at the cost of two to three times more severe hypoglycemia.[^1]

items: **Long-acting analogs vs NPH:** a Cochrane review of 24 trials in type 2 diabetes found fewer hypoglycemia episodes with glargine or detemir, with similar HbA1c[^2]
**Degludec vs glargine:** in DEVOTE (7,637 high-risk adults), severe hypoglycemia occurred in 4.9% vs 6.6%, with no difference in heart events[^3]
**Weekly icodec, type 2:** HbA1c fell 1.55 points vs 1.35 with daily glargine over 52 weeks in people new to insulin[^6]
**Weekly icodec, type 1:** HbA1c matched daily degludec, but clinically significant lows were almost twice as frequent[^7]

blocks.text: Doses are individual and adjusted over time using glucose readings. Type 1 diabetes usually needs both background and mealtime insulin, given as several daily injections or through an insulin pump, often linked to a continuous glucose monitor. In type 2 diabetes, guidelines usually add a GLP-1 drug before or alongside insulin, then start a single daily basal dose if targets are still not met.[^8]

Rapid-acting insulin is injected shortly before (and for some products, right after starting) a meal. Daily basal insulin is given at the same time each day, and the weekly products on the same day each week.[^4]

items: **Hypoglycemia:** shakiness, sweating, confusion; severe lows can cause seizures or loss of consciousness and need glucose or glucagon
**Weight gain** is common when insulin is started
**Skin changes:** lumps or dents where injections are repeated in one spot; rotating sites helps
**Low potassium,** allergic reactions and fluid retention when combined with pioglitazone-type drugs
**Mix-ups:** confusing mealtime with basal insulin, or concentrated with standard strengths, is a known cause of serious errors; pens must never be shared

blocks.text: Since 2020, insulins have been regulated as biologics, which opened the door to biosimilars. Several glargine and aspart biosimilars are approved, some as interchangeable, meaning pharmacists may substitute them for the brand where state law allows.

The two weekly insulins, Awiqli and Onswik, are labeled only for adults with type 2 diabetes, and Onswik's label advises against use in type 1 diabetes because of a higher risk of severe hypoglycemia.[^5] Insulin is also prohibited in sport, so athletes with diabetes need a therapeutic use exemption.

evidence.label: Strong: essential medicine with decades of trial data
evidence.text: Insulin's benefits on long-term complications are proven in randomized trials, and analogs have been compared head to head in large studies.[^1][^3] Differences between analogs are mainly about convenience and hypoglycemia risk rather than blood sugar control.[^2]

faq.q: Are insulin analogs better than human insulin?
faq.a: They control blood sugar about as well but tend to cause fewer lows, especially overnight, and offer more flexible timing.[^2] Human insulins remain cheaper and are still widely used.

faq.q: Can people with type 1 diabetes use weekly insulin?
faq.a: Not on current US labels. In a type 1 trial, weekly icodec caused nearly twice as many significant lows as daily insulin, and both weekly products are approved only for type 2 diabetes in adults.[^7][^5]

faq.q: Is a biosimilar insulin the same as the brand?
faq.a: A biosimilar has no clinically meaningful differences from its reference insulin. Interchangeable ones can be swapped at the pharmacy where state law allows; switching any insulin should still be coordinated with the prescriber.

faq.q: Why is insulin on the anti-doping list?
faq.a: Insulin can be misused to build muscle and is dangerous in people without diabetes, since it can cause severe hypoglycemia. Athletes who need it apply for a therapeutic use exemption.
